title: the seasons
hook: a garden wrung out by summer, then the first rain: the texts split the year into a taking half and a giving half

segments.voice: Yesterday, the seasons: ritu, a season, ritucharya, keeping step with it, and a year that turns six times in the Ashtanga Hridaya. What did your season ask of you? Day one thousand three hundred one.

By the end of a long, hot summer, a garden looks wrung out. The leaves curl. The soil cracks. Even the people tending it move slower, and wilt by afternoon. Then one evening the clouds pile up, the first rain hits the dust, and the whole place smells different. Over the next weeks, green comes back. The classical texts saw the whole year as that kind of rhythm: one half that draws strength out, one half that gives it back. Today: the taking and the giving.
screen: `A GARDEN WRUNG OUT BY SUMMER.` → `THE FIRST RAIN ON THE DUST.` → `ONE HALF TAKES, ONE HALF GIVES.`

segments.voice: The Charaka Samhita splits the year into two halves, each with three of the six seasons. The first is adana, the taking. Late winter, spring and summer, while the sun travels its northern course. Paraphrased, the text says that in this half the sun and the wind grow strong, sharp and dry, and they draw moisture and strength out of the world, and out of people too. The second half is visarga, the giving, or the releasing. The rains, autumn and early winter, while the sun travels south. Here, the text says, the moon is strong, the earth is cooled by clouds, rain and wind, and strength flows back. Notice how the text pictures it: not hot season, cold season, but a pulling-away and a pouring-back. The Charaka Samhita follows that through to the body. Paraphrased: people tend to be weakest at the turn where the taking ends and the giving begins, around the end of summer and the start of the rains, and strongest at the other turn, in the cold months. That changes how a low stretch looks. It isn't a personal failing. If the year itself has a taking half, a tired late summer is partly weather, not character. The giving half, then, is a time to rebuild, not just to recover. The sun's turns matter in Hindu life beyond medicine, too: festivals mark the sun's turn north, among them Makar Sankranti, and some Hindus count the northern course as an auspicious time. The texts take that same turning sky and read it in the body.
screen: `ADANA: THE TAKING HALF` · `VISARGA: THE GIVING HALF` · `WEAKEST WHERE TAKING TURNS TO GIVING` · `A TIRED SEASON ISN'T A FAILING`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: breathe the two halves. Let the shoulders drop. As you breathe out, let it be the taking: let the breath carry away what this season has drained, tiredness, tension, the heat of the week. As you breathe in, let it be the giving: let the breath come back slowly, cool and full. Out, the taking. In, the giving. No forcing either one. Then let the breath go on its own, and notice which half this season feels like. If you pray, you can offer what's been taken and receive what's given. The bell holds the time.
The seasons. In the Charaka Samhita the year has two halves: adana, the taking, while the sun goes north, and visarga, the giving, while it goes south. Today's word.
Your line: the seasons. Today, if you feel low on strength, ask whether the season might be taking, and give yourself one small thing back. Day one thousand three hundred one.

howItsDone: Ayurvedic practitioners describe the year in two halves, adana and visarga, and adjust diet and activity to protect strength in the taking half and rebuild it in the giving half.

options: the taking half of the year, at its low point.
fork.reveal: the text places weakness where adana, the taking, turns into visarga, the giving: around the end of summer and the start of the rains.

original.note: Sanskrit adana: taking. In Ayurveda, the half of the year while the sun travels its northern course.

trapdoor: what you thought: the year is just hot and cold.
what it means: the texts read the year as a taking half and a giving half, and the body moves with them.
what a scholar hears: Charaka's adana and visarga, tied to the sun's northern and southern courses, with strength lowest at the turn from taking to giving.

sources.ref: Charaka Samhita, Sutrasthana 6.4–8 (the year in two halves, adana and visarga, with the sun's northern and southern courses; the qualities of sun, wind and moon in each; strength through the year)
Ashtanga Hridaya, Sutrasthana 3.2–7 (uttarayana as adana, dakshinayana as visarga)

notes: Charaka Sutrasthana 6.4–8 recalled from memory: confirm the assignment of seasons to each half, the qualities of sun, wind and moon, and the strength pattern (weak at the end of adana and start of visarga, moderate in the middle, strong at the end of visarga and start of adana). The script simplifies 'strong' to 'in the cold months'.
'Festivals mark the sun's turn north, among them Makar Sankranti, and some Hindus count the northern course as an auspicious time': confirm wording; no date is given on purpose.
The hook's summer garden is an everyday picture, not a claim about the text.
